note: Hand-specified CJK search expectations. Unlike tests/fixtures/queries.json
this is NOT generated from an oracle: lunr cannot segment CJK at all, so
there is no reference implementation to compare against. Every expectation
here was reasoned about and is explained by its `why`. Changing one means
deciding the old behaviour was wrong, which is the point — a generated
fixture would let a regression rewrite itself.
`expect` lists document refs in required rank order. `expect_empty` asserts
no results. `contains` asserts the refs appear somewhere in the results
without pinning their order, for cases where ranking between them is not

cases.why: The core claim: a two-character term is found inside an unspaced run of Han with no dictionary, because both sides tokenize to the same bigram.

All three contain the phrase; the ranking is the assertion. zh/search carries it in its title and twice in its body, zh/engine once in a body about motors, zh/mixed once in a trailing clause about Rust.
A four-character term spanning three overlapping bigrams. Requires the phrase-verification path, not just bigram presence.
A term that appears only in a body, with no title boost to carry it.
Latin script inside a Chinese index still tokenizes on whitespace, so a Chinese-language index remains usable for code identifiers and product names.
Han immediately following Latin in the same field. A tokenizer that only started a Han run at a field boundary would miss this.
Marz finds the word 'dictionary' without using one.
None of these bigrams occur. Bigram tokenization must not make everything match everything.

cases.why: The phrase-verification case. All three contain the bigrams, but ja/search has them contiguous and in its title, ja/widths has them contiguous in a body, and ja/scattered has 検索 and エンジン as separate words — so it must rank last rather than being excluded.
The name of the technique Marz deliberately does not use, found without using it.

Partial matches rank, they do not vanish. ja/scattered contains 機械 but not 機械学習, and still appears — at roughly 1/127th the score. Filtering it would make a CJK query behave as AND while the same query in English behaves as OR, which is a worse surprise than a low-ranked extra hit.
The document spells it in halfwidth katakana with a combining voiced mark; normalization composes both sides to the same three code points. This is why match positions index normalized text.
The document has fullwidth ＲＵＳＴ. Folding maps it to ASCII, so a user typing on a US keyboard finds it.
The iteration mark is a single Han-adjacent character that a byte-indexed trimmer used to panic on. Kept as a case because the panic was real.
A bigram whose second character is the iteration mark.
No matching bigrams anywhere in the corpus.

cases.why: Korean is written with spaces, so this is ordinary whitespace tokenization — the point is that Marz does not force bigrams on a language that does not need them.
Written as one word in ko/search's body. ko/scattered writes 검색 and 엔진 separately, so a bigram-everything approach would conflate them.
Compound written closed in one document and spaced in its title.
None of these syllable blocks occur in the corpus. Korean tokenizes on whitespace, so this also confirms an absent word is absent rather than partially matching a longer one.
